utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay to continue with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yesterday we broke, Mr. Jatras, when we were looking at the document produced in your first bunch of exhibits, the report of the select subcommittee. Could that be put back in front of the witness, please. It's the large document. In fact, put all the exhibits in front of him, please. We were looking at page 200, which is section 4 of the document, dealing with the conclusions of the select subcommittee, committee on international relations for the US House of Representatives report of October 10th, 1996. Are you at that page, Mr. Jatras, page 200?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The conclusions here, as we know, are those conclusions which have been subject to declassification. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But in paragraph 2, it stated: "The subcommittee feels the need to share with the American people as best it can the results of the investigation." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And there was a hearing in which evidence was heard by the select subcommittee; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Documents produced and witnesses questioned by counsel?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And even those appearing in front of the select subcommittee would have had their own counsel?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be -- generally under an American procedures, that would be the choice of the person, whether to retain counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. The third paragraph: "It is our hope that the administration will relent in its efforts to conceal the history of this foreign policy fiasco, so that they will see a reasonably complete version of the full report." And that's what we have here, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And of course, the blacked out portions are those that the administration would have concealed or removed for release of the unclassified report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The heading of number 1 is: "The administration's Iranian green light policy gave Iran an unprecedented foothold in Europe and has recklessly endangered American lives and US strategic interests." We dealt with the issues that were concerned there to remind everyone, yesterday, which concerned American troops being involved in IFOR and SFOR, as well as the strategic interests. "The Clinton Administration, unable to convince the United Nations to follow its lead in lifting the Bosnian arms embargo and unwilling to abandon its foreign policy philosophy of assertive multilateralism, found itself in 1994 without a vehicle it found acceptable to implement a change in foreign policy it believed to be in the national interest, the lifting of the Bosnian arms embargo. Accordingly, the administration was receptive when its ambassador to Croatia, Peter Galbraith, a man noted by his colleagues for his passionate pursuit of courses, free-wheeling style, and an open attitude towards Iran, pressed policy makers to consider a scheme whereby Iran would be allowed to act as the US surrogate in providing military assistance to the Bosnians." Looking at that there -- in fact, the CIA were not involved in this; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not informed at the time the decision was made, as I understand it. That is to say, it was through White House channels, through Mr. Lake, from Mr. Galbraith, the ambassador in Croatia at the time, and ultimately a decision made by the president, and only after that decision was made were the defence department and the CIA told. What involvement they may have had after that fact, after the decision had been made, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. The policy developed through completely unofficial channels, if you like, in which it was obscured from the eyes of those with interest in the House of Representatives and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I think one thing is worthy of note here, which has bearing on my paper in January of 1997. You'll note in the initial sentences of the paragraph just below conclusion 1 that the committee appears to be criticising the Clinton Administration for not securing an end to the arms embargo or finding some other way to provide weapons to the Sarajevo regime. That is to say, they agreed in substance that we should be helping the Muslims in the conflict in Bosnia. They disagreed with the way it was done through the Iranians. And this is why I believe it did not focus at all, this report, on the other aspects that I saw to bring out in the January 1997 paper, that is to say, the other network which we would now refer to as Al Qaeda and the Islamist orientation of the Izetbegovic government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You had become aware from your research in that exhibit we produced first yesterday that there was another dimension to this, that it wasn't solely Iran which had caught the focus of this particular committee?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And as I said, because of particular American sensitivities surrounding our relationship with Iran, that was the focus of the committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So outside Iran, and this was something I attempted to deal with yesterday, but it didn't make itself clear when I was questioning you, outside Iran, the other interests were what, that was -- that you were able to see were at work within Bosnia in the supply of arms or financial support?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or also bringing in volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: People?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mujahedin. It was the network through the so-called charities, like Third World Relief Agency. It has since been documented after 9/11 in many congressional hearings that are also public record that many other such organisations were involved in this, and at the time it seems there was very little objection raised by anybody on the American side, including, by the way, from the committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now when you say "charities," we probably have in mind here various UN-sponsored charities to deal with health, humanitarian relief, refugee agencies. Are those the sort of charities we're talking about or another dimension in the world of charities?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, and again, I don't want to exceed the scope of what I can directly attest to, but those who are knowledgeable about the global terror network are aware that the funding mechanisms are applied to activities that may include activities of the sort that you describe, in addition to those that are violent, that we would describe as terrorism. This is classically true of an organisation like, say, Hamas, which will support terrorist activity on the one hand, but also then does support schools and the hospitals and things of this sort, so that the activities are mixed up together, and it's sometimes hard to not only trace the source of the funding but even where the funding ultimately is disposed. But again, this is something that is a matter of constant inquiry and public record, not something that I have particular direct evidence of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look, then, at the next paragraph, and I'm going to be concentrating on this particular conclusion and then quickly going through the others. "The president's decision to give Iran a green light in the Balkans allowed Iran to expand its economic and diplomatic relations, as well as establish a military security and intelligence presence so expansive it became the largest concentration of official Iranians outside the Middle East. The consequences have been far-reaching and pernicious. They persist to this day."

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is indeed what the committee found, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to say what was established there in terms when we use -- the expression is used of "military security and intelligence presence." Are you able to give us any idea of the extent or scope of what was established, first of all, on the Iranian part of this issue?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Kay, not beyond what the committee has documented here. As I have said before, the significance of my reports not only here on Bosnia, the January 1997 report, but I would say even more so the reports I did on Kosovo, are the extent to which I have direct knowledge in the sense that this was known or knowable to American officials. This report, in some detail, shows what the committee had become concerned about regarding the Clinton Administration's facilitation of Iranian influence, which the committee found to be quite damaging to American issues, to American interests in the way that you describe. The committee, for reasons I can't explain, since I was not part of their deliberative process, chose not to examine other presences, other assets in Bosnia which I suspected or I believe as a policy analyst should be brought to the attention of the Congress because they were at least as damaging to American interests. My testimony would be direct only insofar as my report is direct contemporaneous, direct contemporaneous account of what was known on not only the Iranian side, which is confirmed in this document, but also the parallel, largely Saudi-supported network and also the character of the Izetbegovic government. I would make the same assertion regarding the papers on Kosovo, beginning with the one in August of 1998, indicating at that time that the Clinton Administration had set itself on a course to intervene militarily in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking at the next paragraph, and I mention it because Croatia is referred to: "In Croatia, a government that had before the green light been a consistent ally in the US's fight against Iranian-sponsored terrorism was co-opted by the weapons it received in exchange for being a staging point for the shipment of Iranian arms into Bosnia. As a result, after the green light, there was a serious deterioration of cooperation with the US, encountering very real and imminent Iranian-linked terrorist threats. The US even now must cope with the consequences of Croatia's developing what has been referred to as an all but out of control relationship with Iran in the wake of the green light." In summary, are you able to tell us what that is about?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Kay, I cannot go beyond the substance of what is stated in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It merely indicates that the Croatia had been used in this means of avoiding detection in the supply of arms to Bosnia through Iranian channels?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what is stated, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It says in the next paragraph, about the consequences being much worse in Bosnia after the green light, Iran virtually overnight became the unrivalled foreign benefactor of the Bosnian government: "As a result, the Bosnian government became less secular and democratic and more open in its embrace of a radical Islamic political agenda, acceptable to Iran but inimicable to US national security interests and democratic values."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Jatras, you should just confirm what is in the report, if you can. And if you have additional comments to make, make them.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I will confirm the factual statements in the report as what they purport to be. The committee examined this issue. They reached certain conclusions. By and large, I would say those conclusions are accurate insofar as this is my assessment as a policy analyst at the time, not because I had direct knowledge of the matters under discussion. In fact, I would quarrel with some of the conclusions, for example, the one Mr. Kay just read, that the increasingly undemocratic Islamic orientation of the Izetbegovic government was a result of this influence from Iran because of the green light rather than an indication of what their inclinations had been for some years, that that was in fact the ideological orientation of the SDA from the beginning of the war. So, but that, as I say, is a policy judgement rather than a matter on which I have direct evidence, and if it please the Court, I would rather focus on the reports which I issued about which I do have direct knowledge, which I believe have direct bearing on the matter of this case, and accept that the public reports which I have -- the committee reports which I have acknowledged in the analyses which I have prepared for the policy committee are, as I have cited them in the papers I prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you'll no doubt take account of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. For reasons at this stage in relation to the Defence, we take the view it's important to read these aspects into the record, and I'm not going to read every word, but I'm going to -- I'm moving through it in a particular way, and then we'll get on to the next stage of this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, it was stated: "Somehow the administration failed to see the short-term expediency of its Iranian green light was a long-term curse on the Bosnian people." That's concerned with the political issues in relation to what had taken place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's stated then in 1996: "Even now the administration is having to cope with the fallout from its policy." Further on in that paragraph: "Iranian influence in the highest Bosnian ruling circles remains pervasive, and Iranian terrorist and intelligence capabilities in Bosnia remain great cause for US concern. The Iranians are biding their time and the radicalised Bosnian Muslim political leadership may yet succeed in turning Bosnia into a radical and authoritarian state." It goes on in the report to criticise the president and those working for him as poorly serving the administration; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what is stated, and again, I would note the careful focus on the Iranians and avoiding mention of other radical assets that may be present at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And in terms of what happened, it's put this way, in paragraph 4: "From the beginning, the administration realised the green light policy was dynamite and so worked to implement it without fingerprints." And in relation to your role and your analysis, would you agree with that comment that what had happened here was a cover-up that was not meant to be generally known?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is certainly what the committee is saying, and to that extent I saw my role as an analyst at the policy committee, admittedly in partisan circumstances, to be, so to speak, dusting the fingerprints that the administration had sought to conceal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This had to be discovered rather than be declared by the government?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had to be discovered initially through press reports so that it became a political issue which then was one that was focused on by the relevant congressional committees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. If we turn to page 204, because this might be of importance: "At the time the administration was making high-minded arguments about the need to respect both internationally agreed upon rules and US allies, it was working assiduously behind the scenes to undermine them." And was that the issue here, that what was happening was in fact not something that was official policy, nor policy that had been recognised as a valid and appropriate policy through the allies of the US?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly, and this relates to a characterisation you made earlier that this somehow was not official policy. Clearly all those engaged in the policy were themselves government officials and had the power, if not the authority, to undertake what they did. At least in American law, one of the questions would be was this technically a covert operation? What laws and reporting requirements was it subject to? It certainly was not one, though, that, as a policy matter and as a matter of our alliance obligations was discussed with our allies or other partners in the international community, except obviously the countries involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did the committee point out a number of public statements that were made by administration officials which were in fact found to have been not true; they were deceptions?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the committee suggests, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And presumably you were aware of these public statements by officials yourself whilst undergoing your analysis?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Secretary of State Warren Christopher: "The United States is not, underline not, covertly supplying arms or supporting the supply of arms to the Bosnian government." National Security Council: "The US did not cooperate, coordinate, or consult with any other government regarding the provision of arms to the Bosnians. We have always made clear that we were abiding by the arms embargo and that we expected other countries to do as well." Again, department of state in response to questioning: "We are certainly not contributing to it and we are certainly not turning a blind eye," the blind eye being what was known and what was happening in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And again, Mr. Kay, I would point out that the committee is very selective in its choice of revelations on this matter, that here, when it refers to Iranian influence, they're quite free in exposing the fraudulent denials by administration officials, but, for example, regarding the numerous reports received by -- numerous reports by allied officers in Bosnia regarding flights landing at Tuzla for making deliveries, this is addressed in both the House and Senate reports simply by way of asking the relevant agencies if they knew anything about them, receiving denials, and accepting those denials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Flights from where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We don't know. You all I can say is, again, not as a matter of direct knowledge, but as an analyst following these reports, some of these are described in the committee report and specifically in the Senate report, which I guess has not been entered into the record, the committees make note of these reports, describe who the officers were making the reports and then show what action they took, which was to inquire of the intelligence community and the Pentagon, receiving denials and accepting those denials. So as I say, they're somewhat selective, it seems to me, in deciding which administration assurances they consider to be lies and which ones they consider to be the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, the issue of the denials and what happened went all the way to the top, didn't it, because President Clinton, in response to a question: If the US was involved in orchestrating the transfer of arms to the Bosnian Muslims, said no?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will not comment on Mr. Clinton's reputation for veracity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: These sources are samples, aren't they, of the denials that you've talked about and were all in various public documents and they're in fact noted in this report?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And you can see some of them are simply cited to media reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In section 7, the administration was criticised for deliberately concealing the truth from Congress regarding the president's Iranian green light decision, and it stated: "Despite protests to the contrary, in the early months of this investigation, deputy Secretary of State, Strobe Talbott, recently submitted to the subcommittee that the administration had intentionally not told Congress of the green light it gave Iran in the Balkans."

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Kay. Where are you looking at here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Section 7, page 205.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Yes. That is what the committee found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So this committee was also being misled. There was the misleading beforehand and then there's the misleading to the Congress committee?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was both public false denials and denials to the relevant congressional committees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Section 8: "Several administration officials gave false testimony to Congress on the development and implementation of the Iranian green light policy."

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in fact, there was a cover letter to this report, one that was submitted to the administration, asking for a justice department investigation of several of these officials. It was responded to by a letter from Attorney General Reno at the time, who found there was no grounds for such investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Congress committee required Ambassador Galbraith be investigated?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They requested it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. But Attorney General Reno did not proceed?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: She did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But the select subcommittee said it was truly disturbed that it received testimony and statements from the National Security Advisor, Anthony Lake, deputy National Security Advisor Samual Sandy Berger, deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott and Ambassador Walker, that directly contradicts Ambassador Peter Galbraith's sworn testimony with respect to material issues before the subcommittee and Congress."

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the committee found, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "The subcommittee is further dismayed that sworn testimony provided Ambassadors Peter Galbraith and Charles Redman, both before the House International Relations Committee and the select subcommittee is not supported by evidence uncovered through this investigation." Are you able to help what that is about?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, not beyond what is stated in the committee report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. In section 9, it says: "Evidence that Ambassador Galbraith played a significant supervisory role with respect to at least one Iranian weapons transhipment shipment through Croatia. Galbraith's goal in facilitating this transhipment was to effect political and military conditions in Bosnia. There is also evidence that he had input or advanced knowledge of the planning and operation of the Iranian weapons pipeline that Iran used to ship arms and gain influence in the embattled Balkans."

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And again, that's in the context of the conclusion there in number 9 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that this may have been a covert operation which has specific consequences in American law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 11, and this is the last passage I'll deal with in this report: "The administration is holding its embarrassment behind the veil of classification."

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you'll see there are a lot of blacked-out sections of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, that's all we need deal with on that issue. And I'll move on in your evidence now to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, your lawyer has been spending the last two hours wasting time, without allowing the witness in actual fact to broach the main subjects that he has direct knowledge of and that he worked and was involved in. And the witness himself said yesterday when he mentioned Al Qaeda and the global network, in respect of Kosovo and Bosnia and so on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've stopped you because we have a procedure that we will follow. You do not set the procedure here. The Chamber sets it. And the procedure is that Mr. Kay is now examining. When he has finished, I will invite you, as I have done before, to consider asking us to allow you to put questions. That would be the appropriate time. Mr. Kay, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And on one matter, Your Honour, as it does need to be addressed: I am here and ready to take instructions from the accused if and when he chooses to do so. I have been put in this position as a result of what has happened in this case, where he has been found unfit, through medical reasons, to represent himself, and without his instructions, I am attempting to put his case as we can see from his opening, from his own cross-examination previously, on the issues in this trial. And documents and exhibits that are produced from his witnesses, which have been made available by his team and have been disclosed in this case are the only materials that I have to go on. And in those circumstances, I have to use my judgement on those materials as the best way to deal with them. And some of the issues raised this morning, it seemed to us, were relevant and pertinent to his defence, because his cross-examination has been on the lines of the Iranian influence in Bosnia, the Mujahedin, and this is a public document that this witness was producing on his behalf as part of his Defence Exhibit material. Now, the witness went on to deal with Al Qaeda and the other terrorist organisations and has been at pains to point out that this is all from his own research, and he wasn't there at the time, and this is as far as it can go. There are other issues about the credibility of those dealing with Mr. Milosevic, and this issue also goes to the US administration at the time, about which we've heard a lot said, and about their comments concerning Mr. Milosevic. So for those reasons, I have embarked on this line of cross-examination, doing my best, without instructions from him. But he's willing to appoint his own lawyer as the order makes entirely clear, and we would encourage that. We have not volunteered for the role that we have been given, but in the circumstances, it seemed appropriate that we were the team to have to pick it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. The Chamber finds no fault with the way that you are examining the witness. The Chamber recognises the difficulty. The situation would have been much better had the accused given you instructions, and the accused will not be allowed to interrupt the examination-in-chief. If he wishes, he can instruct you. And again, if he wishes, he can, at the end, invite us to consider allowing him to put questions. And that's the procedure which we will follow. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On an entirely separate point, Mr. Kay having indicated that he's finished the questions he wants to ask about this document, the Chamber will remember observations made yesterday by me challenging the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond admissibility of the document. I think the Court was very careful in the way it invited the document to be dealt with, it not yet having formally being admitted as an exhibit. Our objections to its admissibility stand. In our submission, this is a document that cannot assist the Chamber at all. It certainly can't support any factual findings of the matters concluded by the committee, nor can it be relied upon, in our submission, to undermine the evidence, for example, of Mr. Galbraith. I will say no more by way of repetition of my objection. It's entirely a matter for the Chamber. Our position is that this is not an exhibit which should be admitted in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will deal with it at the end, but I just pause to say that in my own view, it is very relevant to the case put forward by the accused in cross-examination as to the help that the Muslims received from Iran.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will deal with it at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Much obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking at the other exhibits that you've produced, Mr. Jatras, document number 2, we've considered already, and in it you told the Court in evidence yesterday about how you were looking at the other side, the extra support outside Iran that there had been to the Bosnian government from other Islamic sources. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we also touched on that a moment ago in your evidence, and I have no need to take that document any further. And we shall now move to Kosovo. I've got an order here, which is not my order, how they came to me, and I won't deviate from it because I don't know if there is any great significance. But it's not quite chronological. Document 3 that we look at is dated March the 31st, 1999, and it's headed: "The Kosovo liberation army: Does Clinton policy support group with terror, drug ties?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that a document written by you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And again, that is in your function as advising the Republican policy committee on international relations?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. If I could put that into context. This paper dated March 31st, 1999, while the Kosovo war was under way, was the last of four papers I issued on that topic. Two other ones, dated February 22nd and March 23rd, are also in this group of exhibits here. For some reason, the other paper that is also cited on page 1 of the March 31st paper and in the other two as well was the first paper of the series, dated August 12th, I believe, 1998. I will, of course, comment on these other papers as well, starting with the one you have referred to, but the August 1998 paper is the one I believe is most significant and relevant to the case, in that it describes, in direct terms, the preparedness of the Clinton Administration to attack Serbia in the very near future. As it turned out, six months later. That description was two months prior to the date given in the indictment relevant to Kosovo, that there came into being, it is alleged, a joint criminal enterprise regarding Kosovo. Again, as I've stated with respect to my other papers, they are significant not because they can be taken as direct evidence of the matters described in the paper, but the papers themselves are direct contemporaneous, official assessments about the course of American policy at that time from someone in the American government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's start there, then, and I have not been given, and we were not supplied with that earlier paper in 1998. But you can tell us now, then, going back a year, what the issues were that you uncovered.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the paper, which again you see the title of it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the paper you're referring to, the March 31st paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about three-quarters of the way down the page. It says: "Bosnia II: The Clinton Administration sets course for NATO intervention in Kosovo, August 12th, 1998." I do have copies of that paper, for whatever use you may put them to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I could have a copy of it now.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. And I have one for the Prosecution if they would like one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Judges would obviously need one as well. So --

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe someone should make some copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could make copies.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't know how you want to proceed, Mr. Kay, whether we should come back to that paper after copies --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's start with it there. You're familiar with it and you can tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To summarise what is asserted in that paper at that time, August of 1998, and the reason the paper is titled "Bosnia II" is that it was clear to me as an analyst at that time, and it was clear to me, I contend it should have been clear to others, that the administration had made a decision to intervene militarily in Kosovo, either by creating circumstances where Serbia would consent to an occupation of Kosovo or through undertaking military action to bring about that result, and as I then describe in the later papers, simply the implementation of that plan. Even as of August of 1998, I was able to assert, and I think it turns out, quite accurately, that that course had been decided upon, and the only thing lacking in implementing that course was a suitable trigger, as I refer to it in the paper, quoting an unnamed defence department official mentioned in a Washington Post article I believe in June or July of 1998. So I would say even that plan may have been decided upon by the administration even earlier. The reason I called it "Bosnia II" was that it seemed to me it had all the hallmarks of what we had seen in Bosnia; that is to say, taking a very, very complex, very messy conflict with lots of blame to go around and boiling it down to a morality play, where we had good guys and bad guys. With the evil Serbs and the saintly Albanians and naturally the United States would be on the side of the angels. This entailed other things which I also stated in the August 1998 report and mentioned in the subsequent reports a -- I believe a whitewashing of the character of the Kosovo liberation army, which had been called by American officials, specifically by Robert Gelbard had been described as a terrorist organisation, although it was never, as far as I know, officially listed as one. But if you're going to embark on an invention of claimed humanitarian grounds based on a very stacked presentation of the equities, you have to overlook certain things on the -- with respect to your chosen beneficiary. As I say, I think the evidentiary value is this: You have an official source saying: Six months before the attack came, that there would be an attack, and two months before a joint criminal enterprise supposedly came into existence, which I believe lends credibility to what would -- what would be understood as the normal business of a government, which is to protect its territory and people, not to formulate plans for criminal activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to the Kosovo policy, did you write at all about the extent, how wide the intervention was going to be?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I described the military planning that had taken place up to that time and what appeared to be getting the political machinery in place for proceeding with the intervention. And this was something that primarily related to our NATO allies and what essentially appeared to be a negotiation between our allies and Washington over their reluctance to support air strikes and their insistence that Americans provide a major part of the manpower to be part of the occupation force when the occupation would begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We know that in October of 1998 that there was a cease-fire that was brokered between the KLA and the Serbian government.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The so-called Holbrooke/Milosevic agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. You've dealt with so far the period before then. In terms of the KLA and its influence, as you were able to see on the political machinery in Washington --

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- was there anything you were able to observe?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not -- you're saying the influence of the KLA in Washington?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say this: The Albanian cause in Kosovo, which I don't dispute the validity of in the sense that every nation, every people has its right to its own perspective on matters, clearly had strong support in Washington, but I would say that also extended to a very dismissive attitude toward serious and I would say credible reports of the character of that specific organisation. These are the ones that I gave fullest description to, you can see in numerous, numerous quotes from those sources, in the March 31st paper, that the Kosovo liberation army was substantially, in its leadership, a criminal organisation, let's say tied to Albanian organised crime throughout Europe, really, and also that it had links to terrorist influences, both Iranian and also Al Qaeda, the same kind of people we saw getting their assets into Bosnia during the Bosnian war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the same way that we dealt with issues yesterday concerning Bosnia and the former Yugoslavia and American perceptions of Serbia, in relation to Kosovo at this time, was there an understanding of the significance of Kosovo to the Serbian people, its historical, cultural, and its root, if you like, with the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would on occasion hear people ask questions about that. Again, as an analyst at the policy committee, I would often receive inquiries from Senate offices, generally from staff, but I was on occasion able to brief senators on it who would ask me, you know, who are these people, what is this place, what are the Serbs' interests here, what is the Albanian interest, and so forth. In general, though, given the degree to which Serb had become almost a synonym for some kind of a -- you know, it was almost used like a word like Nazi or something. You couldn't describe in many circles a Serb interest or a Serb perspective on a matter having to do with potential violence in Yugoslavia without immediately decrediting [sic] your argument. In fact, I should note that in preparing my reports I did not use Serb sources for the simple reason that they would be immediately considered discredited. I could possibly use Muslim sources or Croatian sources, certainly European or American sources, but a Serb source was automatically not admissible in that political context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've all now got this document. I've just written an 8 on it to indicate in the chain where it lies. And that might be a useful way of having it. August 12th, 1998, was there any misrepresentation of the sort of organisation the KLA was?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say so much a misrepresentation of saying the KLA is not a criminal organisation, the KLA does not have terrorist ties, but rather a default assumption that the Albanian cause is a just one, they're freedom fighters are freedom fighters and nothing more needs to be said about it except that Mr. Milosevic and the Serbs are clearly the bad guys and we must do something. And again, I think some of those quotes along those lines are given in the paper itself from the Clinton officials. If you look on page 3, for example, that there's a quote from Ambassador Holbrooke, and I think there's another one on page 4 from Secretary Albright. The thesis being that the Serbs - let's say Mr. Milosevic - cannot do what they did in Bosnia, again giving their interpretation of what was done in Bosnia, they cannot now do this in Kosovo, and we are now going to do something about it. That doesn't entail a direct representation or misrepresentation of the Kosovo liberation army. It simply ignores the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There's a paragraph headed "whitewashing the KLA."

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in the second part, you refer to media reports of recent embassy bombings in Kenya and Tanzania may be connected to the deportation from Albania of several members of the terrorist cell of Osama bin Laden.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were the Al Qaeda links to the KLA something that had been observed and pointed out? Were they noted?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly in that article, and again I would refer you to the March 31st paper, and I would not go beyond those reports, again to accept the Prosecution's point, I have no direct knowledge of the accuracy of those reports. On the other hand, I do have direct knowledge that those reports from credible sources were available, certainly they were available to the administration, and there's no evidence the administration took them seriously. I would also note in retrospect, for example, we have a gentleman down in Guantanamo, Mr. Hicks from Australia, who fought in Kosovo before he was arrested fighting with the Taliban against the Americans in Afghanistan. I suggest that a Taliban-oriented Australian didn't end up in Kosovo fighting for the Albanian cause because he was recruited by the Salvation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's go now to the next paper, which we had begun to look at, paper 3, March 31st, 1999. Again, you're writing about the KLA and here tying it in with drug dealing, terror organisations. Is this again information that was being made available in Washington?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was being certainly made available in my report, and given the dates of the sources cited in there, which are not classified or secret sources, they were available to anybody who cared to compile the information. I would note that this report was issued while the war was under way and that the previous reports were issued before the war actually started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And again it points out the Mujahedin and the other aspects, the same aspects you've referred to in Bosnia as having been present in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And if I can characterise what we saw from the green light episode in Bosnia as a reckless disregard for the consequences of such associations. I think the same thing could apply here, noting, by the way, that the reports refer to KLA violence against Albanians as well as against Serbs, and I would say given what happened in Kosovo as of June 1999, when the Serbian forces were withdrawn and the cleansing of Serbs that occurred in Kosovo, I would say that the reports that I sought to draw attention to were very much vindicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Document 4, dated February the 22nd, "Clinton Kosovo intervention appears imminent." This is a follow-on from the earlier article you had written in 1998, when you indicated, on the 12th of August, what the policy was going to be. And was this your characterisation of the issues that were involved in terms of US foreign policy?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And one thing I would note in there is that ten days - excuse me - on -- this was issued on February 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look -- there is a report - excuse me - a hearing in the House of Representatives on February 10th that I cited in there in which a senior Defence department official, Walter Slocombe, was already referring to KFOR by its acronym at that time. So even though supposedly we did not have a Kosovo force until June of 1999, when Serbian forces were withdrawn from Kosovo, at least by well over a month before the war began, the military planning had gone so far as to even have the name of the force we were going to insert into Kosovo once the occupation began.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Document 5, March 23rd: "Senate to vote today on preventing funding, military operations for Kosovo." A paper in this series dealing mainly again with what these issues were, but looking at the so-called trigger event of Racak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I would say this is one of the more significant matters I would like to point out in these papers, which, as I again remind the Court, are contemporaneous, official documents. In August of 1998, I had said that this was essentially ready to go, this was a course that the administration had decided upon and they were lacking only a trigger, some event that would make the operation politically saleable. And I even said in that August 1998 paper that they would do so on the same, I would say, cavalier basis that they used in -- cavalier with regard to the facts, that they used in Bosnia regarding the market-place and the breadline massacres. That is to say, there are events that occur in war that are often at the time very difficult to know precisely what happened. Even when investigation is given, it's hard to know what is happening sometimes. You never know precisely what had happened. That did not change the political utility of such events for the Clinton Administration. As Secretary Albright commented with regard to one of the market-place massacres, so-called Serb mortar massacres, that we don't know exactly what the facts are; therefore, we must believe the Serbs are responsible. This violates not only all laws of logic; I believe it may violate the laws of grammar in the English language, to say "we don't know, therefore." I think the same pattern as I predicted in August of 1998 was followed with respect to Racak. As I discuss in some length in the March 23rd paper, which was issued the day before the bombing began, it was very unclear from the information available at that time what exactly had happened at Racak and that the forensic team, headed by Dr. Ranta had pointedly said: "We cannot say whether there was a massacre at Racak." Maybe there was. I don't know. I wasn't at Racak. I don't know if now, years after the event, anybody is in a position to say with certainty precisely what happened at Racak. The point is that in terms of political intention to move forward with a predetermined plan to attack Serbia, Racak was politically useful and Racak became what the Clinton Administration said it was. If they immediately want to say it was the massacre of an entire village at point-blank range, forced to kneel, et cetera, et cetera, as I have quoted Mr. Clinton and Senator Biden in my paper, that's what it was because it was useful for pursuing a course of attack that they had previously determined upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Document number 6 is a text of a speech you gave on the Balkan war, finding an honourable exit. I don't know actually seek to go through this. I don't know whether you may be questioned on it or whatever, but it doesn't have anything here further than your testimony has been already; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would take it as -- again, this is not an official document. It is a speech given at a public policy institute, a think-tank in Washington, in which I refer to the documents. I think it is possibly useful as a summary of my description of the significance of the documents plus some other material regarding Rambouillet and other aspects that I think buttress my claim made six months prior to the war that the administration had already determined upon this course and well before, it appears, the allegation of a joint criminal enterprise took place. I would say that there are other -- for example, the famous paragraph 8 of annex B to the agreement that was discussed at Rambouillet where it appears that we were demanding not only occupation of Kosovo but all of Yugoslavia. And that, you know, there are other indications we can go into as well, but perhaps not necessary at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: CATO is an acronym of what institute?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: CATO. It is a think-tank. It is -- it has its name, the CATO institute. It is one of the libertarian political orientation generally that supports a fairly non-interventionist perspective on foreign policy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is the abbreviation of what letters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It evidently is not an abbreviation. It's just CATO, yes. I've wondered about that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You mention Rambouillet and in this paper, I mean, I'll look at it as you've mentioned it. I have it on good authority, and I'm looking here at page 3 of the document, in the middle, "I have it on good authority that one senior administration official told media at Rambouillet under embargo, we intentionally set the bar too high for the Serbs to comply. They need some bombing and that's what they're going to get."

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And when I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer. Thank you. A.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will pause between question and answer. As I stated there, "I have it on good authority," that is to say, from confidential sources, not confidential in the sense of classified, but confidential in the sense of people I know who were in a position to know and rather would not identify themselves, that this had been said by a senior official, and I think it's -- whether it was said or not, it certainly describes the situation that I think must be universally acknowledged to have existed, where a country is presented with a demand for occupation of its entire territory or to be attacked militarily. I don't know how one could describe that as not setting the bar too high, unless a country didn't consider occupation to be out of bounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's look at the last document, number 7. It hadn't been one I was going to rely on with any particular detail. We don't have the date because the photocopy cut it off. It's the Navy Times, August 21st nineteen-ninety something or other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it 1995?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. It was faxed on the 25th of August, 2004?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is there any significance in this newspaper extract from Navy Times that you wish to draw to the Court's attention?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only this, and again, I would agree with you, Mr. Kay, that it should not be given great weight because I'm not able to say in great detail what its significance is, and my direct observations on it would be -- direct knowledge about it would be fairly limited. But let me describe it as follows: If you look at the Kosovo war, as was initiated by the Clinton Administration, the legal grounds for it is extremely limited, slim to none, I would say. We did not get -- we, the Clinton Administration, did not get a Security Council resolution authorising it. It did not even get an authorisation from our own Congress. In fact, a resolution of authorisation was affirmatively voted down in the House of Representatives. We did secure an agreement of the North Atlantic Council, again on what basis it's hard to say, in that the North Atlantic Treaty refers only to the defence of the territory of member states and the right of individual and collective self-defence under Article 51 of the UN charter, none of which were at issue in Kosovo. The only thing that could possibly be said for the Kosovo operation - and again, the legal authority for this, I'm still not sure of - would be that it was necessary to prevent a humanitarian catastrophe, that human rights were so violated on such a massive scale, or potentially would be, that some action was necessary. Again, laying aside whether the humanitarian catastrophe ensued after the initiation or when the initiation of hostilities was imminent and was itself among the proximate causes of that humanitarian catastrophe --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was among the causes of that humanitarian catastrophe, my purpose in mentioning that report or alluding to it in my CATO remarks was that with respect to Krajina, the Clinton Administration was seemingly less fastidious about the massive humanitarian hardship when, even in cases where it may have had some direct connection to the infliction of that hardship. This report in the Navy Times, which is a non-official publication but one that is widely read in military circles and in government, refers to air strikes that were directed against Serbian positions in Krajina during Operation Storm. The article refers to strikes against radars. It suggests that carrier-based planes were asked to come to the scene because Pakistani peacekeepers were receiving artillery fire from the Croatian forces, although that's not stated, and that when they came to the scene, Serbian radar locked on to them and they struck at those radar sites. The reason that struck me as significant is it was known from the Serbian side that there were false broadcasts, what we would describe as Si ops, to sow panic among their forces and population and to encourage them to leave flee the scene and flee Krajina. Striking transmitters would have been greatly -- a facilitation of such broadcasts. Inquiry was made, not official inquiry but rather on the part of a retired officer with experience in Vietnam and knowing something from a professional standpoint about the use of air power, that official happened to be my father, as it happens, who called the Congress, talked to people at the Pentagon and ultimately to people at Air South in Naples asking about this report and trying to get a little more information. The response he received was essentially that it was a mistake. There were no such planes, no such operation, nothing happened. It was a mistake. Given the names in the article, the names of the ship, the names of the flight leader, the specifics of the aircraft, it is hard to believe that the entire report is simply a mistake, it didn't happen. I just throw that out there, mention that in the CATO or alluded to it in the CATO remarks, for what it is worth, as an indication given the kind of falsity the Clinton Administration was capable of pedalling on the other matters we've discussed in Kosovo and Bosnia, that their humanitarian claims should also be taken with a great deal of scepticism.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly request that the speaker slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you are asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I'm asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no further questions to ask you, but wait there, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do you wish to invite us to consider allowing you to put questions to this witness? Yes or no. Did you hear the question, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that Mr. Milosevic is waiting for the end of the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, that was the end of the interpretation. Mr. Robinson, there's no sense to this. Mr. Kay himself explained that he was not able to examine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've cut you off. I asked you for a yes or a no answer. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is this: I want you to return my right to self-defence back to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Jatras, just a few preliminary questions to make sure I understand where we are. Did you go to the former Yugoslavia at all in the course of the period with which we are concerned?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion during the Kosovo war, I accompanied a congressional delegation to Macedonia to visit the refugees there, also to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That was the only occasion, was it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you speak the language?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The visit to Macedonia, I suppose, may lie behind an observation you've made about refugees stating that they had fled either because of the activity of the Serbs in Kosovo or because of the NATO bombing; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, no. I was -- again, let me pause. It's contrary to my nature. Actually, no. I was citing -- I was taking those from press reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. So I'm just trying to clear the decks a little bit. It appears you have, therefore, nothing by way of actual, direct evidence coming from the territory that you can help us with?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing, actual, direct evidence coming from the territory. My direct evidence is solely that within the government and the thinking in the government in Washington.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have expressed and indeed been allowed to express conclusions, including general observations on the integrity of the Clinton Administration and indeed the honesty of its president. But this material comes to you simply from public-source material?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Insofar as you have had some access in your job to confidential material, you've cut it out from consideration, so that all you're telling us is conclusions that anybody else could have reached having access to the same public material?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're currently a lawyer for the first time -- first time practicing as a lawyer. How long is that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just over two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you've made some references to legal issues here. You bring no legal expertise at all to the evidence you've given?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say to the extent to which I had a legal education, my service with the State Department and with the Senate was informed by that background and education, but no, that is not a specifically legal perspective on the issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You realise there are different provisions for expert witnesses that prepare reports?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. And I'm not here as an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you're not here as an expert witness as a lawyer, you're also not here as an expert witness in any other capacity because you don't pretend to any special expertise on the matters about which you've been giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not accept that exactly. I would claim expertise on the formulation and implementation of American policy as I have practiced it during certainly my 17 and a half years at the Senate, as well as my experience with the foreign service. However, I am not testifying as an expert based on that experience. I'm testifying on what I knew directly -- what I knew directly was the state of knowledge or reasonable -- facts that reasonably could be understood from the perspective I had at that time, at that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As maybe we understood it, then, we have to draw a distinction between a factual finding and the fact that reference to such a finding or reference to such a possibility was generally abroad?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. And that is the distinction I've sought to make during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So just to take an absolutely straightforward example, you've rather headlined this for us: Racak, was it a massacre, was it a set-up: You are in no position to help this Chamber at all with any conclusion to that as a factual problem?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your ability is limited to saying: But there were papers being distributed about which said this and that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exactly. I would say my expertise, and I would say it was direct expertise, was to say: What was the perspective within the American government, in an area which I have direct knowledge and some expertise, about how the Clinton Administration dealt with that question, which was as unknowable then as regarding the answers and maybe even more unknowable, given its immediacy, than it is today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, because I want to be quite clear about your evidence and how to address the Chamber about it in due course, that last answer rather differs from the answer a couple before, where you said that you weren't testifying as an expert based on your experience in policy and foreign service, you were testifying on what you knew directly, "What I knew directly was the state of knowledge or reasonable -- facts that reasonably could be understood from the perspective I had at that time." You see, we have to distinguish between what I accept you're giving evidence about, things that were discussed, things about which there were papers, and the application of those things that were discussed. So point number one: You've given evidence about things that were being discussed.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You now want us to accept, I think, or in answer to my questions, you're inviting perhaps the Chamber to accept, that you can bring some expertise to bear on how those things available for discussion were relied upon by the Clinton Administration.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again perhaps I'm failing to catch your distinction here. It seems to me that anyone giving direct evidence about the things that he knows, knows things and assimilates information according to his own background experience and degree of familiarity with the events surrounding him. That is to say, I was not, you know, a bricklayer or a physician in the venue as -- in the official venue in which I found myself during the time in question, but rather, somebody who was there, present, who was aware of certain discussions, information that was available from the perspective of someone with my professional background. That is to say, when I was aware of the reports that were available on policy issues and how those reports were dealt with, I was aware of them from a perspective of a person who is himself part of the governing process in the United States, not from somebody who maybe was not familiar with these types of issues. So my direct evidence is from the perspective of someone in a segment of the government at that time and knowing how government deals with these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If there's anything in the evidence that's going to be admitted along the lines of that last answer, and indeed along the lines of the last few answers of his questioning by Mr. Kay, it's material in respect of which a report would have been helpful, and in respect of which I might require time to meet the evidence in due course. We can turn to that if the Chamber is about to have a break, at a later point in time, because in any event I need to read the document that hadn't been produced in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice. We'll take the break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before returning to this witness, I'm asked to deal with an administrative matter relating to the previous witness. Four clips from the film "Death of Yugoslavia," were played. They should have been prepared in advance as separate CDs, in accordance with the prevailing practice. It's my oversight not to have that done. They are now available. They may be given either sequential exhibit numbers or a single number, as the Court decides, probably sequential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That can be done later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. It's just seemed, in case I find anything to produce for this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll look at all the exhibits at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Jatras, before turning to matters of detail, you, of course, understand, I think, that this is a Tribunal that deals with Serbs, Croatians, Albanians as defendants and has no interest in any particular ethnic group. Is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You do. So we are utterly unconcerned about matters of prejudice. Equally we represent and have no interest in any particular government. You understand that as well?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We are here to uncover the truth. Before I look at matters in detail, just a couple of personalities who appeared and you might be able to help me with. First there was the person you referred to in the statement - we don't have to look at it again - the statement of yours, the person in the administration of America who told you that they had intentionally set the bar too high for the Serbs to comply. Can you tell us who that was?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I heard it might have been Secretary Albright but I do not have the exact identity of that official.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It wasn't told to you personally?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, it was not. And I made that clear when I referred to it. It was told to me on good authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My mistake for misinterpreting the statement which makes reference to something under embargo, and I assumed that that was the identity. But you don't actually know who, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If anyone. It may not have been said. I heard from a source that I considered reliable that it was said. If you're suggesting it is mere hearsay, that's exactly right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your source being, please? Your source, please?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: A colleague in the House of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we have his name?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you insist upon it, yes. You do insist?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'd like to have it, unless there's any reason not to.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only that the person told it to me on condition of confidentiality, with respect to his source. And I generally respect the confidentiality of people who tell me things in confidence if I consider them trustworthy individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll leave it there. But mindful of your answer that you, of course, can say nothing as to the accuracy itself of what you were told?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I freely concede that and did at the time I mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second person about whom you just might be able to help me, because it came as a surprise that you mentioned him as your father. His role in this was what?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of professional interest as a man who had served in a military capacity for a number of years, including flying over 100 combat missions in Vietnam, one familiar with the use of air power, and also a person concerned about the course of American policy that was, he felt, distinctly different from the values he thought he was defending in all of his years of professional military service. He simply saw the report and wanted to know more about it and its accuracy and received what he regarded and which I regard as a very implausible answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He was simply making contact as a member of the public?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No particular interest other than as a member of the public and as a former Vietnam combatant?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And with no particular obligation to receive any answer or effectual answer from the persons he contacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Shall we go first to this rather substantial document, because I think we could use some of your assistance on it. You recognise of course that none of us has any particular expertise in the American way of government and we'll need your help. So if we go, please, to the pages just so we can understand this --

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Literally the first page sets out, under -- or over II the select subcommittee members. That's Henry Hyde, and he I think was a Republican; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he still is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Lee Hamilton who is still a Democrat?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And on the left we see Mr. Bereuter, Mr. Burton, Mr. Ballenger, Mr. Meyers - he was a replacement - and I think they are Republicans?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The way committees are organised in our Congress, the majority party always has a majority and all committees and subcommittees and controls the committees and subcommittees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And indeed we can see that at the bottom. It's sort of explained.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Under footnote 1?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you will see of course the list of names on the left which is the majority party Republicans is longer than the list on the right, and that's true of all committees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then so the two on the right are the Democrats, Berman, Bereuter and Hastings with, of course, Mr. Hamilton as the third Democratic member of the committee?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand. Now, we've been taken through, at page 200, some conclusions. But insofar as these are fact finding conclusions they are findings of the committee, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They're not your findings?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You are in no position to express any views yourself, as an individual but --

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not in a position to give direct -- to say I am directly confirming what the committee found. I am able to take note of what the committee found as a responsible actor in our system of government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And of course you realise that all matters of fact here are for the Judges of course?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could we just look, if we've got it, please, at the passage of evidence of Ambassador Galbraith. We've had evidence here from Ambassador Galbraith, as you know, and I hope it's going to appear on your screen. At a time when -- at the time when the accused was questioning Ambassador Galbraith, he said to him: "Tell me, Mr. Galbraith: You spent five years in Zagreb, according to what Chris Hedges from the New York Times says who wrote a text on the 24th of December, 1997" -- I'm so sorry. I hadn't checked that it was working. You have a special place because you did not represent the true state of affairs of Washington and the relationship of the Serbian authorities until the Serbs were expelled, were actually expelled from Croatia; is that right? No. All right. And tell me this, then: John Galvin, the retired general who took part in the negotiations in Yugoslavia, together with Charles Redman, who was otherwise an expert for the so-called doctrine of low-intensity conflicts, was an advisor to Alija Izetbegovic, advisor to boot; is that right, Charles Redman, he was a US ambassador and American representative to the contact group, and I don't think he was an expert on low-intensity conflict. All right. Tell me this, then, please: Is it true and correct that for the Iranian shipments of weapons to Bosnia-Herzegovina, that your president knew about that, Bill Clinton and that Holbrooke, in his testimony to Congress, recognised that arms were being infiltrated into Croatia from Iran? Answer: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is your last question. Your time is then up. And is it true and generally well known, said the accused, that you were included in the affair over the secret import and smuggling of arms into Bosnia, you were involved in that? Answer: Well, first I was not involved in the -- in any way the smuggling of arms into Bosnia. This was the subject, this whole issue was the subject of a number of congressional hearings and reports, as well as a lot of press discussion. And what I did come out in the course of that, and it was very simple, I think it was the 28th of April, 1994, President Tudjman asked me, as I knew he would, what would be the attitude of the United States if Croatia, if Croatia were to accede to the request from Bosnia to permit arms from Iran and from other countries to transit Croatia, to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I told him, on instructions, of course, that I had no instructions, which he understood to mean that the United States did not object and indeed the arms went, shipments went forwards. And then he goes to deal with some other matters of the Clinton Administration.
