But that evidence that he's given this Court is the same account that he gave to the committee, in broad terms, and indeed we can see the letter in -- or a letter or memorandum of his in the document setting out his position; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at the next document. This one I think may be new. I haven't -- it may actually be in these 700 pages but I haven't been able to find everything yet. This, therefore, must be produced as potentially an additional exhibit. And this is again, just so that we can see it at the best form, this is the position taken by Ambassador Galbraith before your committee -- or not your committee, the committee; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This committee, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Expressing his gratitude at the opportunity to appear. I shan't read all paragraphs. But his position to your committee was: Two years ago, the Bosnian government asked the Croatian government to permit the transit through Croatia of weapons for its beleaguered army. The principal suppliers of these arms would be Iran. The Croatian government asked for our reaction. The administration decided we wouldn't answer, and I told the Croatians I had no instructions. The Croatians understood this response and a subsequent colloquy described to you by Ambassador Redman to mean that we would not object to their role in helping the Bosnians. I believed then, and even more strongly now, that the administration made the right decision. Because of the arms, the Bosnians were able to survive. Eventually, the outside arms which came from countries -- which also came from countries other than Iran enabled the Bosnians to redress the military imbalance with the Serbs, recover some territory, and thus pave the way to Dayton. The next paragraph he sets out casualties to date. In the following paragraph, he deals with a matter involving Ambassador Redman. He says that the Bosnian people left unarmed against the Serb aggressors had barely survived the winter of 1993/1994. Without help, we doubted they could survive another year. This was then the context for our decision. Let me explore for a minute, said the ambassador, the consequences if we had said no. Under these circumstances, I think the very fragile Muslim-Croat Federation would have collapsed, that the Bosnians would have doubted the sincerity of their Croatian allies. And I don't want to take too long because it's going to be available to the Judges. But if we go to the next page in the paper version, he said: "I do believe," top of the page, "a unilateral lifting of the arms embargo would have provoked the Bosnian Serbs to move against the essentially undefended enclaves." Now, that was his position before the committee, and again, as you see, it's the position in summary he gave before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the views he expressed there, Mr. Jatras, the views about the consequences of not arming the Bosnians, were views that were indeed being considered in Washington?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As he states in his letter, the decision to lift the arms embargo to overtly take action to arm the Bosnian Muslims, was something that was debated. The secret arming of them via giving a green light to the Iranians, as I recall, was something that only became a matter of public debate after the press accounts began to emerge that this was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He, in his evidence - and indeed as we're going to see in a document - dealt with this on instructions in the oblique way of saying we have no instructions.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And as the committee makes clear, it was understood on the Croatian side what the meaning of that "no instructions" instruction was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now let's go back, if we could, to the report. Because we've looked at page 200, at the conclusions, very strong conclusions of the committee. Well, it's not actually the conclusions of the committee, is it? Because although you didn't explain this, it's the conclusions of the majority?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exactly. Even though the majority has a weight in preparing the report, they generally will consult with the minority and take their views into account. Again, I'd have to look through the committee report to see by what vote it was adopted, but you will generally see a vote in the committee to adopt the report --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you find it for us now?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I'd have to look through this rather lengthy document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can perhaps come to it in another way, I suspect. Because you can help us with the way of government in America. This is a fact-finding committee, composed of members of Congress?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Senators?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Congressmen?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: House members. Excuse me, sir. There is also a Senate report which I also cited in my January paper, which evidently is not in evidence. I can give that to you if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it -- even in a fact-finding exercise, is it common for a committee to divide entirely on political lines? Is that what happens?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, without looking at this record, I do not know that the committee did divide on political lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Okay. Because --

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the way, if it did, there would be a substantial -- well, if you look on page --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're going to come to it in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we do, can we, in order to go through the document in a methodical way, just look at page 220. The Judges may find this helpful in the setting of the evidence in this trial, because this particular document, although it's been subject to redaction, no doubt, for reasons of sensitivity of confidential material, is a memorandum of Ambassador Galbraith, contemporaneously 1994, and again, setting out, we needn't go through it all, the same account, the account of saying that they had no -- he being instructed they had no position to say no and therefore replying that the answer was they had no instructions. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that's --

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not keeping up with your reading as quickly as you're going through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 220, if you can find it.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So this particular document from Ambassador Galbraith --

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Memorandum to file.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Consistent with his evidence here. Would you like to turn over to the following page, please, which is number 223. Now, this is minority views.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we see this is submitted by Messrs. Hamilton, Burman and Hastings, who were of course the three Democratic members; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So we haven't yet found the vote. You may be able to find that for us; I don't know. But if we then turn over to the following pages, to guide the Judges through the immediate following pages through this very substantial document should they want to find anything else in it, we see there's an index, and that's an index, isn't it, starting at page 226, for the minority's views?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. So in fact the minority published an extensive report. This isn't a partially dissenting view. This is a full dissent, effectively?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So if we could turn now to page 232, the page numbering is a bit confusing, Mr. Jatras. It changes part way through and we can deal with that, but at the moment we're still on the same sequence of page numbers. The executive summary sets out how the House of Representatives voted to establish and fund this committee. Next paragraph, authorised to investigate and report. Next paragraph, following minority views to the report of the select committee, based on a thorough review of thousands of pages of classified and unclassified materials made available by the department of state and defence, the CIA, National Security Council, as well as press reports and so on. Then it sets out the legislative history. Then we go to page 234, go through treatment of confidential and classified information. And then at 236, we come to the summary of the key findings and conclusions of the minority members who happen to be the three Democrats. And I read the sum in any event of what's here as the conclusions Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the majority have been read out: "The central issues of the select subcommittee investigation include whether the United States government ordered, organised, or otherwise encouraged, Iran or any other country to ship arms to Bosnia, whether the United States government provided a foothold for Iranian operations in Europe, whether the United States government engaged in covert action, without meeting the legal requirement to inform Congress, and how the United States policy regarding the arms embargo affected United States relations with NATO allies. The consequence of United States policy are not in dispute. In 1994, Bosnia was embroiled in a brutal war." I move on to the end of this page, foot of this page: "Based upon the select subcommittee investigation, the minority finds that, one, from the outset of the Clinton Administration, it was United States policy neither to oppose nor support third-party arms transfers to Bosnia-Herzegovina. This policy was embodied in the no-instructions response to the Croatian government's question on the United States' view of the transhipment of arms. It served several important United States interests and helped establish conditions on the ground that pointed the way to peace. During the entire period in which the United Nations arms embargo against the former Yugoslavia was in effect, United States policy was to refrain from supplying arms to any party in the former Yugoslavia. Pursuant to UN Security Council resolutions, the United States agreed in 1992 to participate with its allies in Operation Sharp Guard for the primary purpose of interdicting contraband destined for Serbia. Beginning in January 1993, following the inauguration of President Clinton, United States policy was neither to oppose nor support the shipment of arms to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina from other countries, including Iran. In November 1994, following the enactment of the Nunn-Mitchell Amendment, United States officials informed United States allies that the United States would participate in Operation Sharp Guard for the sole purpose of interdicting contraband destined for Serbia, in compliance with the Nunn-Mitchell Amendment. The United States would take no action to interdict arms destined for Bosnia or Croatia. The no-instructions policy served important United States interests. The outgunned Bosnian Muslims received arms that helped them survive until such time as the circumstances were ripe for a negotiated peace. The United States avoided a confrontation with NATO. The peacekeeping force and humanitarian aid workers remained in Bosnia. No United States ground troops were forced into a combat situation, and conditions were established that paved the way for the Dayton peace accords in November 1995." Over to page 238: "Throughout the period of the United States arms embargo, Iran and other Islamic countries supplied arms to the Bosnians. During the entire period, the United Nations arms embargo against the former Yugoslavia, all parties to the conflict in Bosnia received arm shipments in violation of the embargo. During the entire period of the United Nations arms embargo, the Bosnian Serb military arsenal dwarfed that of the Bosnian Muslims and Croats. Beginning in 1991, several Islamic countries, including Iran, began supplying arms to the Bosnian Muslim forces. The supply of arms to Bosnian Muslims declined from summer 1993 to spring 1994, due to the war between the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croat forces. The supply of arms to the Bosnian Muslims increased in spring 1994 due to the Federation agreement to end the war between Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat forces and the delivery of the no-instruction response. A number of Iranians in Bosnia peaked before the spring of 1994, remained constant until the Dayton peace accords, and subsequently declined to the handful that is present today." Next, the conclusions, Your Honours, go on just to the following sheet, and in fairness to all involved, I think I should probably read them. Conclusion 3 of the minority: "The United States took no action to aid arms transfers to the former Yugoslavia. At no time did any United States government official take any action to supply arms to any country or entity covered by the UN arms embargo. At no time did any United States government official undertake any covert action to supply arms to any country or entity covered by the embargo or to encourage, aid, or assist in the shipment or transfer of arms to any country in the former Yugoslavia. The proposal to expand the pipeline of arms destined for Bosnia through Croatia originated with Bosnian and Croatian government officials in the wake of signing the Federation agreement in March 1994. No United States government official coordinated, cooperated, conspired with, or suggested to Bosnian Muslims, the government of Croatia, or the Bosnian Croats, that the United States be asked to state its views of the transhipment of arms. United States government official directed ambassador to Croatia Peter Galbraith to respond that he had no instructions, when asked for the reaction of the United States government to the transhipment of arms through Croatia to Bosnia by the government of Croatia. Ambassador Galbraith carried out his directions correctly and promptly. No-instructions response achieved United States objectives and was consistent with United States policy. Shipment of arms to Bosnia was not obstructed. The UN Security Council resolution was not violated and serious conflict with the allies was avoided. 4: United States government did not engage in any covert action and was not legally required to inform Congress of its diplomatic exchanges with governments in the region. However, Congress should have been better informed about the no-instructions exchange. Information about the shipment of arms by Iran and other Islamic countries through Croatia to Bosnia was made available to members of Congress on dozens of occasions through press reports, intelligence reports, briefings, and in connection with staff and congressional travel to Croatia. The administration responded accurately to every question from Congress about the shipment of arms to Bosnia from Iran and did not set out to mislead members of Congress. As a policy matter, however, the administration chose not to inform Congress about the delivery of the no-instructions response. The no-instructions response to the question posed by the government of Croatia was a traditional diplomatic exchange. The administration does not routinely disclose to Congress sensitive diplomatic exchanges between ambassadors in foreign governments. The failure of the administration to inform Congress formally about the exchange among Ambassador Galbraith and Special Envoy Redman and a senior official of the government of Croatia is not a violation of United States law. As a matter of policy, the administration should have considered informing selected members of Congress about the delivery, the no-instructions response.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down, Mr. Nice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you're being asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I apologise. There are a few more headlined conclusions, Mr. Jatras. If you think that in fairness to the position that you've expressed, you'd like any of them read in full, just say so. The headlines are, 5: "The impact on the Iranian arms shipment on the security, United States military and civilian personnel was minimal." Conclusion 6: "The impact of Iranian arms shipments on United States allied relations." 7: "The executive branch has acted properly in reviewing actions by United States officials and in responding to inquiries from Congress concerning the arms transfers." 8: "Lapses in communication and coordination among United States government officials in Zagreb and Washington led to confusion and erroneous impressions about United States policy among some United States government officials."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then it turns to a summary of the investigation. So what we see, Mr. Jatras, is that this very substantial document actually presents the views of five men, on the one side, and the view of three on the other. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a great extent, that is correct, unless, as I say, and I have not been able to find it, I find the margin by which this committee report was issued, which has a bearing on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Jatras, if you find it and I haven't managed to dig it out in the time available, I shall be only too indebted to you.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll just look at a few more passages in this document, maybe, to get the picture. If you'd be good enough to go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, may I just ask: To whom does this report go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is sent initially to the administration. It would be, in fact, there is a letter here, I believe, that would be the issuance letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there any greater significance attached to the majority view than to the minority view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally, yes. The committee report is generally to be considered the majority report, and the minority report is what it suggests itself as being, is the view of the minority. They're both accorded great weight, but the majority vote is usually considered "the committee report," with the dissenting views of the minority. And that's true regardless of which party is in the majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the report is the report of the majority with the minority expressing their --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And together they can be considered the report, but generally greater weight is given to the majority report. Again, as I mentioned to Mr. Nice, I would want to see how -- remember, this is a report of just a subcommittee, a select subcommittee, within the International Relations Committee, which has a far larger membership. And I do not see anything here in this tome that suggests how that was voted out of committee and whether it was a straight party-line vote, which it may well have been, or whether it was different from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've seen that the minority's view is headed on a piece of paper with the three minority names, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I mean this is not a legal document. This is in part a fact-finding document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a fact-finding document from a legislative body, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I mean again, I don't want to make an obvious point, but America is different from other countries. We know that courts sometimes divide on apparently political lines, but fact-finding bodies by juries have to be unanimous, don't they?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, yes. Actually, under our system, not in all cases, but generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look at page 205 just very briefly. Part of the minority's finding, the last part of 205: "The minority concludes, had it not been for this rampant speculative reporting, the May 1994 convoy would not have been -- would have been no more significant than the thousands of other convoys that traversed the region during the war." Then this: "The allegations of misconduct and possible covert action were wholly unsupported by any evidence and should not have been accorded the level of significance that was afforded them. The minority also believes" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, is it not 250?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. It's page 467 at the top and the numbering has then changed at the bottom. I think what happened was that the minority report was presented as a separate document with its own sequential page numbering. And it was then integrated into this single document, and so at this page we have two numbers. I'm so sorry. 467 at the top, 205 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I've been reading from the last paragraph, and I can take the second and third sentences: "The allegations of misconduct and possible covert action were wholly unsupported by any evidence and should not have been accorded the level of significance that was afforded them. The minority also believes that the CIA must do a better job of distinguishing between speculation and gossip in intelligence gathering, speculation by the DCM..." DCM, Mr. Jatras?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deputy chief of mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. "...about Special Envoy Redman was rumour and gossip, not intelligence." And if we can then turn on, again using the page numbers at the top, to page 477. "The minority found," top of 477: "No credible evidence exists to confirm the speculation by the United States government officials, by someone, that United States government officials were colluding with Iran on weapons. In fact, the speculative, incomplete, and inaccurate nature of the reporting created suspicions within the CIA that a covert operation, spearheaded by Ambassador Galbraith, was under way." This was wildly disproportionate to the facts. That's another finding by the minority, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And would you now, please, go to page 578 at the top, 317 at the bottom. I don't, I think, need to read all of this, but it's a specific response by the minority to the majority conclusions regarding false testimony of witnesses' classification and executive privilege. And so if we look, for example, at the foot of page 3 -- sorry. Page 578 or 317, we find this approach, this reflection of the reality of this committee: "The most inflammatory aspect of the majority report is its referral on certain matters to the justice department for further inquiry. The majority asserts that several executive branch officers gave inconsistent testimony to the select subcommittee and suggests the possibility that some of these officials might have perjured themselves. This reckless allegation is wholly unsubstantiated. It casts aspersions on the character of dedicated public servants who performed their duties in difficult and at times dangerous circumstances for what we can only assume to be the majority's short-term political advantage." Now, that shows us, doesn't it, Mr. Jatras, part of the reality of a committee like this, it is a political committee, asserted by some, including its own members, to be serving political ends at the hands of the other side?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is certainly part of the reality, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And indeed, it may be that the Chamber, if it wants to have a couple of other pages in mind in evaluating this document, would like to go to pages 624 and 625, although it may need stronger spectacles or a magnifying glass to read them, and in my version they're upside down, but I make absolutely no complaint of that. And on page 625, I'll just read a couple of paragraphs, one paragraph on the following page, and I am done with this document. At 625, in very small text: "This unprecedented legislative procedure proposed, and it gives the authority, was created for one purpose and for one purpose only. It is a political fishing expedition designed to embarrass the administration by creating a perceived problem where one does not exist. It is an expensive political ploy designed to manufacture campaign fodder in an election year. It is a perfect example of politics at its worst." Two sentences into the next paragraph: "No laws were broken. There were no reporting requirements on the part of the administration, no government officials participated in in any prohibited activity and no charges of wrongdoing have resulted from this particular incident." Unless I'm advised to the contrary, we can go for to the next page, page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let me follow the line of your examination. Is it your position, then, that this being a document, which is nothing more than the views of five men representing one party and three men representing another party, which has divided on political lines; it doesn't offer any help to the Chamber in determining the facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would go further and have by my earlier objections all right, I think, set out my position. Fact-finding decisions by another body on issues that are for this Court, if these issues are for this Court, is -- are of no value in the decision making function of this Court, because it is for this Court to decide matters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They could be persuasive. It's for the Chamber to make what it --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If at best it could be persuasive, when it appears to be nothing more than the majority vote of five against three, it would probably be of no -- it would be very hard to justify making a preference for the five against the three. That point is even stronger when it is apparent that the division appears to be along political lines. Yes, those are my observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jatras, on the issue, as you've presented it, about what was known and knowable, do you see a significant difference between what the Republican position was on that and what the Democrat position was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the significant differences are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think there's, to start with, a very significant agreement in the majority -- in the minority views, and I think that the -- again, at the risk of providing an opinion rather than direct testimony, with Mr. Nice's indulgence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Court's indulgence, I would think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and the Court's indulgence. That it is clear from the account of both the majority and the minority that Ambassador Galbraith gave his no-instructions response to the Croatians and that the Croatians took that to mean something. They then disagree on the interpretation of the significance of that. For example, did it or did it not result in a re-initiation of the Iranian pipeline? The Democrats seemed to argue that it was of minimal impact, which one may accept if one chooses to do so. The Republicans seem to believe it was a more significant development. There is a great deal of argument, and again this is purely a matter of American domestic law about whether this is technically a covert operation or not which then would have been statutorily under requirements for reporting in a certain way with congressional committees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But is that not an internal American domestic issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. And regarding the different opinions of the majority and minority, the -- I notice the minority uses some fairly strong language in characterising the majority in how it went about its business and the extent to which it may have been politically motivated, and one could easily draw the opposite inference, which is the Democrats here are with some heat politically defending their administration having been caught in rather unfortunate circumstances. I would also note one other area of agreement, and that is the neglect of both the minority and the majority to address the other issues I sought to address in my January 1997 paper, namely, the non-Iranian participants in bringing weapons and also fighters into Bosnia just demurely noted here as "other countries," and also the character of the Izetbegovic regime in Sarajevo, which even the minority notes was -- Iranians present in Bosnia as early as 1991, that is to say, even before Bosnia declared its independence, so it could not have been purely a product of the necessity to procure arms from somewhere. So I take even the minority's views of something of a confirmation of the picture I sought to present in my January 1997 paper, if some want to suggest there's a partisan aspect to it, well, welcome to the American political system. But that aspect is there. But just as in a courtroom situation, we have Prosecution and Defence. We don't dismiss the arguments made because each side is presenting a point of view which is in the interest of their party, the word being used in a somewhat different sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last passage I'll ask the witness about, page 627, the following page. Their conclusion: "If the majority feels this incident must be examined, then they should do so through the existing mechanisms and committee structures of the House. Should be deliberated in a matter that is responsible and done out of genuine concern over the existing policies with regard to embargoes and third country actions it should not be investigated as a political agenda to be used for election year gains." That's over the names Joe Moxley, and then other names. Can you explain that, it forms a minority view of another report, I think, but you must explain it to us. We can see the beginning of this report at page 620.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me see who that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It will help us with what we've been looking at.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The committee on rules. I must confess, my knowledge of House procedure is not as detailed as my knowledge on Senate procedure, since I've only served in the Senate. The Rules Committee does not perform the same functions in the Senate. What I will -- again, just looking briefly at this, what appears they're suggesting is that the set-up and structure and authorisation of the select subcommittee of the International Relations Committee should have been subject to a different rule giving its authorisation. Again, noting the partisan question you have raised, Mr. Nice, I think this is a shorthand way of saying, from the Democratic side, this should have been done in a way that we were able to block it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Jatras, you appreciate, don't you, that if this document, as His Honour Judge Robinson has raised as a possibility, should ever have persuasive effect as to factual matters, it's essential to know that it is only the conclusion of a majority, that there was a strong minority?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you bring no, as we've already explained, ability to make factual conclusions of your own? I'll simply make this point. It's unfortunate, do you accept this, that you didn't draw to our attention that there was this minority view to an entirely contrary effect?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was unfortunate at all. I can explain if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My purpose, again, in testifying is to elucidate and explain the extent I can the documents that I issued from the policy committee, not to explain the preparation and the weight of every source that I cited in preparing those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cited the House report, I cited the Senate report, I cited a 1995 report from Lieutenant Colonel John Sharay [phoen] from Fort Leavenworth. I cited many press reports. There are facts again from serious sources, including this one, that deserve to be given note of. But, as I said at the outset, I think there are deficiencies in the way that the report was presented, frankly, by both parties, in that there are sensitivities in the American government regarding Iran and whether something is a covert operation and they would have devoted particular attention to those things, and they would have neglected other things which are impolitic, or were certainly impolitic prior to 9/11 to note regarding other radical activities present in Bosnia, and it seemed that in drawing attention to those things which, as knowable, and indeed you note even the minority mentions the press reports as a means by which these activities were knowable to Congress anyway, seemingly in defence of the Clinton Administration neglecting to officially inform Congress. So again, I will note the report is here. It is a partisan report. It contains many assertions of fact that the two parties agree on and others on which they disagree. And that's normal in our system.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Jatras, you're asserting your even-handedness and we do have one of your, as it were, raw documents before us. We've got tab 6, and perhaps we can just look at that for an example of indeed your even-handedness, before I look at another couple of matters in detail.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I did not assert even-handedness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. You don't. You are yourself partisan?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a partisan --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In what sense partisan?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I identified myself as a Republican at the outset.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But that's the only way in which you're a partisan?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it's the only way. I obviously would have sensitivities about my own party that I don't have about the Democratic party. Again, in a courtroom, you try to be fair-minded and factual even though you represent one side of an issue under dispute. And I would describe my role in our partisan system in similar terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's just look, then -- have you got tab 6 there?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we go -- you set out, the Judges may not have had a chance to consider it, set out the rationale on page 1 for the then policy. Page 2, we come to the nutshell and you try and paraphrase things. And then the third paragraph you say this: "To start with, pre-1989 Kosovo was hardly the fantasy land of ethnic tolerance and pro-intervention caricature that it's made out to be. Under the 1974 Tito constitution, which elevated Kosovo to effective equality with the federal republics, Kosovo's Albanians exercised virtually complete control over the political administration -- provincial administration. Tens, perhaps hundreds of thousands of Serbs left during this period in the face of pervasive discrimination and the authorities refusal to protect Serbs from ethnic violence. The result of the shift in the ethnic violence that accelerated during this period is the main claim ethnic Albanians lay to exclusive ownership of Kosovo. At the same time, Albanian demands mounted that the province be detached from Serbia and given republic status within the Yugoslav Federation. Republic status, if granted, would in theory have allowed Kosovo the right to declare its independence from Yugoslavia," and so on. Now, just leading on, yes, one of the ironies of the present Kosovo crisis is that Milosevic began his rise to power in Serbia in large part because of the oppressive character of the pre-1989 Albanian rule, symbolised by the famous 1987 rally, where he promised the local Serbs: "Nobody will beat you again. In short, rather than Milosevic being the cause of the Croatian Kosovo crisis, it could be said -- it could be as correct to say that intolerant Albanian nationalism in Kosovo is largely the cause of Milosevic's attainment of power." So you set that out strongly, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you ever consider Soluvic's [phoen] filmed account of how they went prepared with stones to throw at the police in order to generate the riot that allowed Milosevic to say "we will not be beaten"? Have you considered that piece of evidence?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. If we go on to the next page, then, I've dealt with the source and I'm not going to pursue that any further. But at the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond bottom paragraph, you make this point: "Fifth, nobody can doubt there are serious atrocities being committed in Kosovo by Milosevic's forces, though the extent and specifics of the reports that the media, as in Bosnia, treats as established fact." Your view?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My view is, is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your view at the time?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My view at the time, and my view today, would be that it would be rare indeed, and indeed I think impossible, to find a counter-insurgency war, or war against a terrorist's internal enemy, where they are not atrocities committed on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I am pointing to here is that the cause and the extent of those atrocities are not necessarily the way they're being presented by the Clinton Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Over two pages, please, and then we come to the second paragraph, which starts off with the word "tenth." "Tenth, the notion that Milosevic's nationalist bent on creating a Greater Serbia is nonsense. Milosevic, unlike the equally thuggish Franjo Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic, is an opportunist who likely would have been more than willing to sell out Kosovo as he did the Serbs of Krajina and parts of Bosnia." Your view?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the statement stands for itself. I think again part of the backdrop to the American interventions in Yugoslav crisis was to put horns on one side and halos on the other side, and it seems to me that whatever mistakes Mr. Milosevic made are of a kind or in a question of degree compared to the adversaries, his adversaries in Croatia and Bosnia rather than of a different quality altogether. That is to say, I think some of the quality of political leadership throughout Yugoslavia could have been better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You appreciate we have no interest in the history, save to -- insofar as it informs us about where crimes were committed.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally. And you understand here again I'm giving a policy speech here at the CATO institute. It's not -- you know, this is not direct eyewitness evidence of anything. It is my assessment, as I state at the outset, both personally and as a foreign policy professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last page of this speech, and very nearly the last part of the speech, in the second-to-last paragraph you quote Madeleine Albright, where she suggested that the leader of some countries, Serbia among them, "Try to grab the truth and leash it like a dog, ration it like bread, mould it like clay, their goal being to be create their own myths, conceal their own blunders, direct resentments elsewhere and instil in their people a dread of change." And you turn that saying: "However that is true of Slobodan Milosevic, the Secretary of State should look in the mirror," allowing the qualification for both?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would simply note that the ability of the Clinton Administration to manage information and what we call spin is legendary in both parties in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now, only -- the other documents I have very little to ask you, save to draw to your attention or to the Judges's attention, but I think it's already clear, they are all Republican policy documents, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They are partisan?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the one we've had today for the first time - and I've only had a chance to look at it briefly - is the one that comes in August 12th of 1998, where you set out what you think is going to happen, so that you, as it were, forecast events. What was revealed to you was premised on the fact that there were already grave wrongs being committed against Kosovar Albanians in 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please explain your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go -- let's look at the bottom of the first page. My mistake, the question I asked you. Have a look at the bottom of the first page, where you set out your thesis. "That the administration is waiting for a similar trigger in Kosovo is increasingly obvious. Senior US Defence department official who briefed reporters on July 15th noted we're not anywhere near making a decision for any kind of armed intervention in Kosovo right now. One thing that might trigger a policy change, I think if some levels of atrocities were reached that would be intolerable, that would be a trigger." The position as presented and somewhat publicly presented was that things were bad, if they got worse, then action would be required?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one way to put it. I don't think that is accurately reflective of what I was saying in the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you would accept in any intervention by one state in the affairs of another that there will be a level of wrong or bad things being done by the other party that can be acceptable, it can then rise to a level where it is unacceptable and intervention is required?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I accept the premise of humanitarian intervention as it is sometimes called without the legitimating authority of a Security Council resolution or other legal mechanism, but accept the principle as you've stated it --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I would nonetheless say that there is a duty, just perhaps a moral duty if not a legal one, to ensure that one is not simply taking the kind of unfortunate wrongs that will be committed I think inevitably on both sides of guerrilla insurgency, indeed a terrorist insurgency, and the defending state and to seize upon one and immediately package it politically to serve a predetermined goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. In coming to give evidence here today, just help us with this: Did you volunteer or were you recruited, to the extent I can ask you the question.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked to appear by attorneys --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. That's all I need to know.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course, it's very important, isn't it, Mr. Jatras, that any particular interests that a witness such as you have are properly presented to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So if we can just look at a couple of matters of detail. A bit more about your father, please. He is, I think, by origins, an American, full American, by birth, or what?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you trying to qualify me in ethnic terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born in the United States, and my parents were born in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Going back?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My grandparents were born in Greece.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your parents are still, I think, of the Greek Orthodox faith?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as am I.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As are you. And that faith, to some degree, informs your judgement, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it does, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move on to see whether it does and to what extent it does, tell us this: There are, of course, Serb communities in America, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you mix with them, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have many Serbian friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you mix with the Serbs in America where they are collected together in Serbian organisations, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have on occasion, yes, not as a regular matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the views that you hold, which is why I was careful to establish that you were holding yourself out as even-handed, and you qualified it, but never -- the views that you hold, Mr. Jatras, when you raised them with the Serb expatriate community, are standard views, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you're not in any sense an extremist, are you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Extremist in what respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In any of the views you hold?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that the views that you hold and that you set out at various meetings and in various speeches are the sort of views that the Serb community you mix with finds acceptable?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not my understanding that the members of the Serbian community, or any other community in the United States, have uniform views.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us a little bit, please, about the Serbian Unity Congress. The word "unity" suggests what?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent to which I am familiar with the organisation, which I am not a member of, they are a Serbian ethnic fraternal organisation of the sort that are quite common among ethnic communities in the United States, one of I think three or four major Serbian organisations in America.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is your father a member?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is he a supporter?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he's conversant with them, but he is not a member. If he has joined, I'm unaware of the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is he a donor?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he donated on the occasion when I spoke at their congress in nineteen-ninety -- I can't remember the year. It was possibly 1999, 1998. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Money raised by Serb expatriate communities such as the Serbian Unity Congress in the time of these wars went to serve what purpose, please?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it primarily again, since I'm not a member of the organisation and don't look at their books, my best understanding is that it goes for essentially two purposes: One, to support the organisation's activities in the United States, which are largely informational and fraternal, that is to say, they support a website and distribute information; and secondly, I understand they do provide some relief to refugees in Bosnia, people have come to Serbia from Bosnia, Kosovo, so forth, blankets, food, sweaters, things of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You know I'm not asserting it, I'm just asking you. Do you know if any money raised served any purpose of buying arms, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know of it and I would strongly doubt it. And I could tell you why I strongly doubt it if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: . Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly because we have something in the United States called the Neutrality Act which makes it criminal to do that and I would note in that regard that nobody has ever accused the United States government of being friendly, for example, toward Fidel Castro's Cuba but organisations have raised support for illegal violent actions against his government to have him prosecuted under the Neutrality Act. I note that the supporters of the Kosovo liberation army freely recruited fighters and raised money in support of the KLA, and as far as I know no action was ever taken against them. I doubt that forbearance would be shown toward any Serbian activities of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Can we now, please, look at a document of yours. It will have to be given another exhibit number. Did the last document, the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. The last document that we produced, which was the submissions of Ambassador Galbraith to the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If you were to give 781 to the footage of the video you've shown, and 782 will be the one given to the -- this statement, the next number will be 783.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we now, then, please, look at the next document, which I think you will recognise, Mr. Jatras, as a speech of yours, or I beg your pardon, an article of yours. We can see that this is something headed: "A journal of Orthodox opinion. The Muslim advance and American collaboration." It's clear from the heading that although it was published later, it's adapted from a May 1998 speech you gave called -- headed: "Overcoming the schism. European division and US policy," at a conference organised or sponsored by the Rockford Institute and The Lord Byron Foundation for Balkan Studies. If we look at the first paragraph, Mr. Jatras, you say, in line 4: "...the Islamic resurgence that has rapidly come to mark the post-Cold War era. For the east which borders on the Muslim, the problem continues to be, as it has been since Islam first appeared in the seventh century, primarily one of direct, violent confrontation, which today stretches from the Balkans to the Caucasus and through central Asia. For the west, on the other hand, the problem today is primarily internal both in terms of ideological confusion (which in many instances leads to active collaboration), coupled with demographic infiltration." Still your view?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's quite a factual description, and I -- since the writing of this article and especially after 9/11, a great deal more information of that from Islamist sources is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We then see in the next paragraph your depiction, no doubt in order to excite emotion, of 100-acre Islamic academy gracing the rolling hills of the Virginia horse country, and you comment on the role of the Saudis in the school that was proposed. If we go over the next couple of pages, we come to what is page 3 of 8 at the top, and these are your ideas on Islam, so that we can just understand them. Page 3, the very wonderful systems for displaying material occasionally take a second or two to move between pages. I'll just read this passage out. It's on page 3 of 8, and it reads as follows: "Likewise, the idea that Islam shares with Christianity and Judaism an Abrahamic pedigree, that we are all, in the Islamic phrase, peoples of the book, is now almost universally accepted. To see how flimsy this idea is, suppose that during the early Christian era, a pagan philosopher from Athens had claimed to have received a vision from a divine messenger to the effect that Jupiter, the Greco-Roman father God, was the one and only God and in fact was the same God the father preached by the Christians," and so on.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please pause, Mr. Nice, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is part of your approach to the divisions or separateness of religious in our world?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm making a theological observation regarding the assertion, which I believe is unfounded that Islam shares a common origin with Christianity and Judaism but rather is an outgrowth of indigenous polytheism on the Arabian peninsula.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at the foot of the page, indeed, to see how you depicted it on this paper. Last two lines: "In short, Islam is a self-evident outgrowth not of the old and new covenants but of the darkness of heathen Araby. Beside ludicrous historical suggestions to the contrary (such as that the Ka'bah was built by Abraham, which would have been news to him), Muslim apologists have strained to find in the Bible evidence that a new prophet would arise after Jesus, seeing Muhammad in obvious prophecies of the Holy Spirit," and so on. And if we go to the next paragraph, beginning, "Saint Gregory's," this: "...answer is no less devastating to Islam's fraudulent self-depiction as a pacific creed. Islam was born in violence, from Muhammad's sanction of raids of pillage and plunder (starting with attacks against his own Quraysh tribe, which initially rejected his revelation) to his savage execution of hundreds of men on the Qurayzah clan (which professed Judaism) and the enslavement and enforced concubinage of their women and children."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause to let the interpreters catch up, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you're again being asked by the interpreters to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if we look down to the next paragraph and to the middle of it, we see these views of yours expressed in the form of a rhetorical question --

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page are we on, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 4 of 8, the paragraph in the middle headed: "In the application of Jihad." You say: "The parallels are unavoidable to the similarly Manichaean communist concepts of the socialist camp as the zone of peace and the capitalist camp as the zone of war. I will leave it to the specialists to calculate which Islam or communism can claim the greater achievement as gigantic Christian-killing machines." I must ask you, Mr. Jatras, whether it has ever occurred to you that expressing views in such a way is irresponsible.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you like me to supply the documentation for my assertions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you -- it's a simple question. Do you take the view that expressing opinions in this way is responsible?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is responsible to give testament to something that is historically accurate. There is a reason why there are no indigenous Christians in north Africa west of Egypt, there is a reason why there are longer indigenous Christians in Anatolia. They did not disappear because of earthquake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I ask you the question of responsibility, you think it's a good idea to draw these facts, if they are facts, and I'm not here to debate them, in this way?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think facts are their own justification, whatever they may say, however unpleasant they may be. I would note that what may seem shocking here - and perhaps I think you would suggest somehow not responsible - are commonplace on many expressions of Islamist ideology, stating them in terms not too different than I have stated them here except in a positive and proud way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And there is also historical evidence, you say, to support the view that Islam is the outgrowth of the darkness of heathen Araby?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And if you want to express -- I would make two points. I am a Christian, and even in Christian terms we often refer to the state of my former polytheist ancestors as one of spiritual darkness and the adoption of Christianity as enlightenment. Again, I don't know if in Europe one may speak in these terms. Certainly in the United States, in a Christian context, it is permissible to do so. It is also permissible to criticise a faith. We have feminists, for example, who are not shy about describing Christianity as a terrible, oppressive, patriarchal system, and they're perfectly free to do so. As far as the pagan origins of Islam, I would simply point out that there is no historical evidence of Abraham having built the Ka'bah, but Muhammad himself refers to his Meccan relatives and the cult that was then established as shirk [phoen] as idolatry. I think that's proof in itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I don't know how much longer you'll be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A couple more minutes probably because I think there is one more sheet of paper that I'm going to need to produce as an exhibit. If the Court is minded to take the adjournment now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the adjournment now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jatras and Mr. Nice, I've had what I might call an official complaint from the interpreters. They're unable to follow, to follow you, and you must observe each pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I've been shown, I think it's a red card almost by the interpreters, and I've apologised to one personally and I'll get around and apologise to the rest. I'm always happy to be corrected, and I realise that sometimes the problem is I make it impossible for them to intervene even to correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Jatras, the fault is mine, not yours. And I will, in the remaining few minutes of questions, set a slower pace. Just three more passages from this document of yours, the article headed: "Orthodox opinion." If we can go, please, to page 6 of the document, right in the middle, you'll see a paragraph that begins, "for example," and reads as follows: "In 1993 statements were issued by a number of Roman Catholic, Protestant, and Anglican spokesmen in the United States urging military intervention on behalf of the Islamic regime in Sarajevo. We are convinced that there is no just cause [sic] to use force to defend largely helpless people in Bosnia against aggression and" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you say that there is no just cause?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is just cause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My apologies: "...to defend largely helpless people in Bosnia against aggression and barbarism that are destroying the very foundations of society and threaten large numbers of people, wrote the chairman of the United States Catholic conference..."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Mr. Jatras, I want to be sure I understand your article. The sentence that I am about to read is, I think, your sentence rather than the report of somebody else's. That sentence, or phrase, for it is preceded by a comma, reads: "At a time when the Muslim beneficiaries of the called for intervention were not only roasting alive Serb POWs impaled on spits, but were slaughtering Roman Catholic Croats by the hundreds in an offensive in Central Bosnia." Was that your sentence?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does that refer to the Muslims in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have evidence, please help us so that we can track it down and use it, for people being roasted alive on spits?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had seen photographs which I understood to have been taken by a Japanese photographer of one particular POW in Bosnia that had been roasted alive on a spit, and I had heard accounts from people on the Serbian side of similar atrocities. I should preface this with a response to your earlier question about whether I had travelled to the region. No, I had not, but I did regularly receive people in my office from the region, including people from Croat and Albanian and Muslim opinion, or communities, as well as people from the Serbian community. I did receive more visitors from the Serbian community, including in their time Mr. Labus, Mr. Djindjic, Mr. Kostunica, and many other political leaders obviously opposed to Mr. Milosevic. The point I'm making there is consistent with the observation I made earlier in my official documents, that is, that an ugly war, with lots of atrocities, was presented as a morality play, where one side had a monopoly of guilt and suffered nothing. I should point out regarding the Croats in Central Bosnia, I did visit a receive. In fact, he visited the foreign relations committee, and I was at the meeting on the foreign relations committee with committee staff at that time. His name was a Mr. Pegarcic [phoen]. He was an advisor to Mate Boban in Herceg-Bosna, and he was describing -- and again, this was in 1993. I'm trying to remember the exact time frame. I believe it was for spring or summer. This would have been the time that we've seen in the documents related to the green light that the -- there had been a falling out between the Croats and the Muslims in Bosnia, and the Muslims had conducted an offensive, including Jihad fighters against the Croats, and great atrocities were being committed. I can tell you that there was virtually no interest in --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't want to stop you for fear of it looking as though I'm seeking to cut you off, but I think your answer is longer than is required by the question I asked. And if I can bring you back to the significance of the question, it's this: You are, of course, an educated and articulate man, are you not?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is some opinion to that extent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're capable of creating quite a reaction in an audience, as we will see, when you make public speeches. And I just want again an answer to my earlier question. Do you think that on the basis of the material coming to you, and of course if it exists and we've got it, we'll find it, we'll use it in the appropriate cases if we can, but do you think it's appropriately responsible at a time of religious or ethnic conflict to present a picture in this way on the material available to you not only roasting alive Serb POWs impaled on spits, do you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is comparable in no way more worthy of fault than the kind of hyperbole that was common at the time in support of the Muslims as innocent people being killed merely on the basis of their religion by Serbs, which was the nature of the discourse at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two wrongs making a right even from an educated person like yourself?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not concede at all that it is a wrong. I think it is a characterisation of the fact that there was -- and again you may find numerous Muslim sources of information on this. It was considered a Jihad land by the kind of assets that were becoming present in Bosnia in part with, I believe, since again I was not there, but according to the reports available, in part with "stealth cooperation," according to the one Washington Post article.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at the foot of the same page, for the second-to-last reference on this document, six lines up from the bottom, in comparing religions: "But it is beyond me what spiritual values any Christian has in common with someone whose idea of beatific bliss is..." the word reads, and I have no immediate translation for it for the interpreters, "...boinking an endless parade of well-rounded houris said to inhabit the Muslim paradise." I think we can guess, but you must tell us. What does the word "boinking" mean in this article?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. It is a word that describes the sexual act in, I would say, crude but not obscene language, deliberately chosen for that reason. Because my point, since we've chosen to indulge in an exercise in comparative religions, is that there is a, I would claim as a Christian, a difference in the moral and spiritual content of what a Christian expects in the afterlife and is standard depiction - and again I would advise you to consult Muslim sources commonly available should you search for them and including, by the way, the justifications given by suicide bombers in places such places as Israel about their expectations for performing as a Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond shahid [phoen]. So I would say yes, it is a crass observation, but the thing I am observing is crass and consequently so is my language for making the observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last page, please, and indeed last four lines. This is your thesis: "At the same time, in light of the growing volume of Muslim immigration, western Christians will soon find out - maybe sooner than they think, given western birth rates - that confronting the Islamic advance has become, as it has always been for eastern Christians, a simple matter of physical survival. But by that time, it may be too late for the west as well." In that passage, you are referring to differentials in birth rates between Muslims and Christians?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Birth rates and also patterns of immigration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you are, I must suggest, generating fear, and that is the purpose to which you put, certainly in this article, your intelligence?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would again advise you, Mr. Nice, to consult Muslim sources saying exactly what I have stated there, with the intention that within the approximate period of time, some decades, the United States, Britain, and other European states will become "Shari'a" states once a sufficient demographic mass is attained. That may not be a picture that is politic to point out, but it was not I that made the point of formulating such a vision. I'm simply calling attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: An alternative approach to what you say is your desire is this, isn't it, that by generating adverse views of whole groups of people - in this case Muslims - you start the process of dehumanising them when you view them as a block subject to unappealing characteristics?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am speaking about an ideology.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you answer my question. It has the -- and you know what I mean by dehumanising. Speaking of people in this way starts the process of dehumanising them, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If what you were saying were true, that would be true, but that is not correct. On the contrary, sir, it is -- if you read the literature from the Muslim side about what exactly is the status of "adeni" under "Shari'a", it is the potential "adenis" who are dehumanised. And that is exactly what -- again, in my role as a policy committee I would often receive visits from people from Sudan, from Egypt, people who were subject to "Shari'a" law in their present lives. They're dehumanised under an ideological system that I think has some very negative consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Come back to dehumanisation on the topic of this case in about five minutes or less. May this exhibit have an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 783, the new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One more exhibit, a single sheet, which we can distribute. I'm afraid it hasn't been put on Sanction. While it's being distributed, just to remind us all, the Greeks and those of the Greek Orthodox persuasion have a proximity in religion, as well as territory, with the Serbs, don't they?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And indeed, with the Montenegrins?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. And Bulgarians and Russians and Georgians. Yes, we are of the same faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the document that's now available and may be displayed on the overhead projector is a document of the Serbian Unity Congress. It comes off their website, I think.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps we can put it on the overhead projector as well. And it describes how there was the banquet at the conclusion of the convention of the 18th to the 20th of October, 1998. Greetings for the banquet were received from the Crown prince and from president Milo Djukanovic of Montenegro. George Vojnovic was greeted with much applause. The dinner included a presentation to Stella and George Jatras, your parents. In special recognition, the Serbian community in the United States, Stella is a tireless campaigner for the Serbian cause. The highlight of the dinner was the keynote address by James Jatras, foreign policy analyst on the Senate Republican policy committee. In a speech of dazzling eloquence and soaring images, he blasted the administration's whole policy towards Serbia, stating that it was criminal and worthy of being brought to The Hague Tribunal. He spoke movingly of the union between American, Greek, and Serb core values and how these had been betrayed by the administration. He urged Serbs to hold on to their sacred vision of the heavenly kingdom."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Nice. The Chamber can't find the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry if I've been reading the wrong excerpt. It's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the right picture, wrong text.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They've distributed the wrong one. I'm so sorry, Your Honour. We had two broadly similar documents. I'm only using one of them. I'm sorry I didn't check. While it's coming around, then: We've heard that the former president, Milo Djukanovic of Montenegro, was present, your parents were present and warmly and especially welcomed, your mother being a tireless campaigner for the Serbian cause. And in your keynote address, delivered with dazzling eloquence, you stated that the administration's policy was criminal and worthy of being brought to The Hague Tribunal. You spoke movingly of the union between American, Greek, and Serb core values and how these had been betrayed by an administration. You urged Serbs on to their sacred vision of the heavenly kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I take it, as I suggested earlier, Mr. Jatras, that the sort of views you set out in your paper document were acceptable to your audience?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which article?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, we've only got the account of your speech.

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not referring to the official reports from the Senate?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, no. My mistake. The document we were looking at earlier, the document headed "A journal of Orthodox opinion," contains a number of your views, and you told me already that these would be your views -- would be views acceptable generally to the Serb people. At this speech of yours, did you raise those sort of views and find them acceptable to the people?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, no. The speech of which I do not have a text, it was from improvised notes on a spontaneous basis, was specifically about, as it says, the spiritual values of the Serbian people, how those relate to my own American and also Greek identity, and again, if you read -- you neglected to read the last sentence about electrifying speech, eloquence and there was something else about something lofty values or something of that sort. These are not my words, of course. It's the website's characterisation. I mostly spoke in that vein. I obviously did not get into the details of the theory and practice of Jihad for the last 14th century, so I don't know to what extent in specific anyone in the audience would have had knowledge of that article or, you know, would have agreed with various parts of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to repeat the point, that the sort of views you've been expressing in writing would be acceptable generally?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The generally accepted thing that I think would be universal in the Serbian community in the United States is that they have been treated unfairly by American policy and singled out in an unfair way for the blame of the violence in the Balkans in the 1990s and their own sufferings had both -- at the hands of their local adversaries and at the hands of the United States, have been minimised and I think that is a fair observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One more quotation, about three more points, and I shall be done. Is it right that on an occasion you have asserted that Michael Dukakis, one-time I think American presidential candidate was pagan for not following the Orthdodox Church on issues such as abortion? Is that the way you would describe him, as a pagan?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly would, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to what this case is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can that be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You came here, Mr. Jatras, to give evidence essentially in relation to Bosnia section of the trial about the arming of the Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES JATRAS [Resumed]
